did_you_know.text: The term 'tamid' marks the regular daily burnt offering — a sacrifice made every day as part of the routine worship.
The phrase 'between the evenings' refers to the time from late afternoon to sunset, so the second daily offering takes place in the evening.
'A tenth of an ephah' is a unit of flour — the rule specifies an exact measure for the meal offering, not just a vague amount.
The text says these offerings were ordained 'on Mount Sinai' — presenting them as part of the divine instructions given to the people at Sinai.
A 'nesech' is a libation — wine poured out on the altar as part of the sacrifice. Rituals included liquid offerings as well as animals and incense.
On the Sabbath two extra lambs are offered as a burnt offering — an addition that marks the special holiness of the day beyond the daily sacrifices.
'Rosh ḥodsheichem' means the beginnings of months in the lunar calendar; the new moon involved special offerings and was observed as the start of a new cycle.
The 'goat for sin' is a goat designated as a sin-offering — here it appears as part of the regular sacrifices serving an atoning function.
The 14th of the month is Passover, and the 15th begins the seven days of Unleavened Bread. The first day is a 'holy convocation' when work is prohibited.
The requirement that offerings be 'without blemish' means the animals had to be flawless — the community was expected to present the best and most complete offerings.
